status: complete — selective across chapters 34-52; see coverage_note
note: The longest book in the canon at 1,364 verses, indexed in sections along its own seams: the call and early oracles (1-10), the confessions (11-20), kings and false prophets (21-29), the Book of Consolation (30-33), the fall narratives (34-45), and the oracles against the nations (46-52). This file covers the first section.
sectioning_note: Sectioning is a practical necessity, not a claim about the book's unity. Each section is indexed against the same standard and validated the same way, and the file's status field names what is done. A reader should be able to see at a glance that the index is partial rather than inferring it from the absence of entries.

entries.pericope: Before I formed you in the belly, I knew you
entries.connection: The objection raised is inadequacy — I don't know how to speak, I am a child — and it is answered by removing the question of adequacy rather than by disputing it. Formation described as preceding the person's awareness of it, which is why C25 treats growth as something already underway before it is noticed.

entries.pericope: What do you see? A branch of an almond tree
entries.connection: The prophet is asked twice what he sees and told he has seen well, before he is told anything. Perception trained by being questioned about the ordinary — a branch, a pot — rather than by being given a vision he could not have looked at himself.

entries.pericope: What unrighteousness have your fathers found in me?
entries.connection: The indictment opens by remembering the kindness of her youth and then asking what fault was found. Grievance framed as a question about the injured party's own conduct, which is the same move Micah 6:3 makes and the opposite of how accusation usually begins.

entries.pericope: Two evils: the forsaken spring, and broken cisterns
entries.connection: Two evils, not one: leaving the living water, and then the labour of cutting cisterns that cannot hold it. Holy Detachment argued from futility rather than from asceticism — the effort is real, the workmanship is real, and the container leaks.

entries.pericope: Your own wickedness will correct you
entries.connection: Consequence described as self-administered — your own wickedness corrects you, your backsliding reproves you — and then the denial is quoted back: I am not defiled. Interior Diagnosis blocked by the one thing that defeats it, which is a confident account of one's own innocence.

entries.pericope: Yet you said, I am innocent
entries.connection: The claim of innocence is made with the evidence still visible on the skirts. The Moral Audit shown failing at the only point where it matters — not from ignorance of the standard but from a verdict reached before the looking.

entries.pericope: Only acknowledge your iniquity; return
entries.connection: Return is commanded four times in three verses, and the single condition attached is acknowledgement — nothing else is required first. The Failure Recovery Protocol with its terms stated at their lowest: name it, and come back.

entries.pericope: Break up your fallow ground; don't sow among thorns
entries.connection: Already cited in the curriculum. Ground is prepared before anything is planted, and the alternative named is not barrenness but sowing into thorns — effort that produces a crop which is then choked. The circumcision of the heart in the next verse locates the fallow ground precisely.

entries.pericope: My anguish; I can't hold my peace
entries.connection: The prophet's body registers the judgment he is announcing — pained at the heart, unable to keep silent. Sacred Lament performed on behalf of people who are not lamenting, which is the form it takes when the sufferer does not yet know what is happening.

entries.pericope: Run through the streets and see if you can find a man
entries.connection: He looks among the poor and excuses them as untaught, then goes to the great men who do know the way — and finds the same thing. An honest search that refuses the easy conclusion that ignorance explains the failure.

entries.pericope: Eyes that don't see; my people love to have it so
entries.connection: The chapter ends by naming the audience's complicity: prophets prophesy falsely, priests rule by their own authority, and the people love to have it so. C08's fruit test given its hardest form, because the deception is jointly maintained rather than imposed.

entries.pericope: Peace, peace, when there is no peace
entries.connection: The wound is healed superficially by declaring peace over it. The Architecture of Peace defined by what counterfeits it — a settlement announced rather than reached, which is the failure C15 is built to prevent.
entries.review: PR09 added before publication — caught by the build-time counter-example check, not by a reviewer. The prose named the Architecture of Peace and the practices array was empty. A wound healed superficially by declaring peace over it is precisely the failure the practice exists to prevent, so the tag was owed.

entries.pericope: Ask for the old paths, where the good way is
entries.connection: Four verbs in order — stand, see, ask, walk — and then rest is promised to those who do. The Two Ways offered as a question to be asked at a junction rather than a doctrine to be accepted, and the refusal recorded is flat: we will not walk in it.

entries.pericope: I have made you a tester of metals
entries.connection: The prophet is given the office of assayer, and the refining is described as failing — the bellows blow, the lead is consumed, and the dross does not separate. Testing that reaches an honest negative result, which C08 has to allow for if the test is real.

entries.pericope: Don't trust in lying words: the temple of Yahweh
entries.connection: A list of what they do — steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely — followed by standing in the house and saying they are delivered. The proof test of C12 applied to religious security itself: the building is real, the assurance is sincere, and neither is evidence.

entries.pericope: I didn't command your fathers concerning burnt offerings
entries.connection: Sacrifice set aside in favour of one instruction — listen to my voice and walk in the way I command. The same reduction Micah 6:6-8 performs, reached by a different route and arriving at obedience rather than at three requirements.

entries.pericope: The stork knows her appointed times
entries.connection: No man repents saying what have I done, and the contrast drawn is with migratory birds keeping their seasons. The audit question is quoted exactly and recorded as unasked — the Moral Audit shown by the absence of the single sentence that begins it.
entries.review: PR01 and C04 added at review. Verse 6 quotes the audit question itself and reports that no one asks it, which is a counter-example anchor under the standing rule.

entries.pericope: Is there no balm in Gilead? Oh that my head were waters
entries.connection: Three movements without resolution: the question about the balm, the wish for endless tears, and then the wish to leave his people altogether. Lament that includes the desire to abandon the people being lamented over, recorded without correction.

entries.pericope: Take heed of your neighbor; trust no brother
entries.connection: Speech described as a drawn bow and a deadly arrow, with peace spoken while ambush is intended. The same collapse of trust Micah 7:5-6 records, located specifically in the tongue rather than in the household.

entries.pericope: Let him who glories glory in this, that he knows me
entries.connection: Wisdom, might, and riches are each disqualified as grounds for boasting, and what replaces them is knowing a God who exercises lovingkindness, justice, and righteousness. The nearest parallel in the prophets to Micah 6:8 — a triad again, and hesed named first among the three.

entries.pericope: They must be carried, because they can't go
entries.connection: The idol is described by its manufacture — cut, plated, nailed down so it will not topple — and then by the fact that it must be carried. What a person leans on is shown to be something they are actually holding up.

entries.pericope: The way of man is not in himself; correct me, but in measure
entries.connection: Two admissions in consecutive verses: a man cannot direct his own steps, and correction is asked for with a limit attached. The Discipline of Unknowing applied to one's own agency, and the request for measured correction is asked rather than assumed.

entries.pericope: I was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter
entries.connection: He is told about the plot rather than discovering it, and the admission is that he had not known. Interior Diagnosis performed on him from outside — the danger he could not see in his own village was the one nearest to him.

entries.pericope: Why does the way of the wicked prosper?
entries.connection: The complaint is prefaced by conceding the point — you are righteous when I contend with you — and then made anyway. Sacred Lament conducted without withdrawing the concession, which is what separates it from accusation.

entries.pericope: If you have run with footmen and they have wearied you
entries.connection: The answer to the complaint is not relief but notice that harder is coming — horses after footmen, the swelling of the Jordan after the land of peace. Gradualism stated as escalation, with the present difficulty reframed as the early part of the training.

entries.pericope: The linen belt hidden by the Euphrates
entries.connection: The belt is worn against the body, then buried, then found ruined — and the point made is clinging. C11's abiding given a physical figure whose failure mode is separation followed by rot rather than by dramatic loss.

entries.pericope: My soul will weep in secret for your pride
entries.connection: The warning is issued publicly and the grief over its rejection is kept private. Sacred Lament conducted where no one will see it, which is the Hidden Life applied to sorrow rather than to good works.

entries.pericope: Though our iniquities testify against us, work for your name's sake
entries.connection: The prayer concedes the charge in full and then appeals to something other than merit. A recovery plea that does not argue innocence and does not despair either, which is the narrow ground the Failure Recovery Protocol occupies.

entries.pericope: The prophets prophesy lies in my name
entries.connection: Jeremiah defends the people by blaming their prophets, and the defence is rejected — both are held responsible. C08's fruit test extended to the hearers: being deceived is not treated as exculpating when the deception was welcome.

entries.pericope: Woe is me, my mother, that you have borne me
entries.connection: He states that he has neither lent nor borrowed and is cursed by everyone anyway. Lament that includes the observation that the suffering is undeserved, which the text records without correcting.

entries.pericope: Will you be to me as a deceitful brook?
entries.connection: He describes eating the words as a joy and then asks whether God will prove to be a stream that dries up in summer. The sharpest accusation in the confessions, and it follows immediately from the account of delight — the two are not in different moods.

entries.pericope: If you take out the precious from the vile, you shall be as my mouth
entries.connection: The answer to the complaint is a condition: return, and separate the precious from the worthless, and then you may speak. Restoration offered with discrimination as its requirement — the audit is what qualifies him, and it is asked of the accuser rather than the accused.

entries.pericope: Don't enter the house of mourning; don't go to the house of feasting
entries.connection: He is forbidden marriage, mourning, and feasting — the three occasions on which a community gathers. The Citizen-Stranger at its most costly: a man kept present in the town and excluded from every ordinary rite in it.

entries.pericope: The heath in the desert, and the tree planted by the waters
entries.connection: The blessed tree is not spared the heat; it does not fear it, and its leaf stays green through drought. Abiding described by what it withstands rather than by what it avoids, which is the same correction John 15 makes about pruning.

entries.pericope: The heart is deceitful above all things; who can know it?
entries.connection: Self-knowledge is declared unavailable by ordinary inspection, and the searching is assigned to someone else. The Moral Audit's necessity and its limit stated in two verses: the examination is required, and it cannot be completed from inside.

entries.pericope: Heal me, and I shall be healed
entries.connection: Healing asked for as something only received, with the recovery stated as complete before it has begun. The petition then turns bitter against his persecutors, and both halves are kept.

entries.pericope: The potter and the marred vessel
entries.connection: The vessel is marred in the potter's hand and made again — not discarded, and not repaired on the wheel where it failed. The Architecture of Growth given its plainest image, and the clay's condition is what determines the shape rather than the potter's disappointment.

entries.pericope: They have dug a pit for my soul
entries.connection: He recalls having stood before God to speak good for them, and then asks that their children be given to famine. The confession that most resists being made edifying: intercession remembered and vengeance requested in consecutive breaths, preserved without comment.
entries.review: PR06 added at review. He recalls interceding for these people and then asks that their children be given to famine — retaliation requested outright, which is the practice being abandoned. PR15 was proposed alongside and declined: harshness is present, but Non-Retaliation is the specific refusal, and one precise tag serves better than two loose ones.

entries.pericope: Pashhur put Jeremiah in the stocks
entries.connection: The chief officer of the temple beats the prophet and confines him overnight. Opposition arriving from inside the institution rather than from outside it, which is where C17 locates the stranger's actual difficulty.

entries.pericope: A burning fire shut up in my bones
entries.connection: He says he was persuaded and overpowered, that the word has made him a laughingstock, and that holding it in is worse than speaking it. Lament that names God as the cause of the trouble and continues anyway, ending in praise without having withdrawn the charge.

entries.pericope: Cursed is the day in which I was born
entries.connection: The confessions end here, immediately after the praise of the previous verses, with no resolution and no return. Habakkuk closes with yet I will rejoice; this closes with why did I come out of the womb. Scripture preserves both endings, which means Sacred Lament is not required to arrive anywhere in order to be legitimate.

entries.pericope: Deliver him who is robbed out of the hand of the oppressor
entries.connection: The instruction to the palace is administrative before it is devotional — justice executed, the robbed delivered, no wrong done to the sojourner, the fatherless, or the widow. The throne's continuance is made conditional on it.

entries.pericope: He judged the cause of the poor and needy; wasn't this to know me?
entries.connection: A king who builds by unrighteousness and pays no wages is set against his father, who ate and drank and did justice. Then the sentence that reframes everything: judging the cause of the poor is named as what knowing God consists of, not as evidence for it.

entries.pericope: Both prophet and priest are profane
entries.connection: The prophet's own bones shake at what he has to say about prophets, and the corruption is located inside the temple itself. C08's fruit test applied where the tester and the tested share an office.

entries.pericope: If they had stood in my council
entries.connection: The false prophets are identified not by doctrine but by outcome — they say peace to those who despise, and no one turns from their evil way. The test given is whether the message turns people, and behind it a claim about where the message came from.

entries.pericope: Isn't my word like fire, and like a hammer?
entries.connection: Let the dreamer tell his dream and the one with the word speak the word — the distinction is left to be made by what each does. Chaff and wheat separated by weight rather than by inspection.

entries.pericope: Amend your ways; as for me, I am in your hand
entries.connection: He delivers the sermon that gets him arrested, then tells the court to do with him as seems good, adding only that killing him would bring innocent blood on them. No defence entered, and the princes rule in his favour.

entries.pericope: Micah the Morashtite prophesied, and Hezekiah did not put him to death
entries.connection: Elders save his life by citing a precedent from a century earlier, and the narrator then records a second prophet who was extradited and killed. Both outcomes preserved, so the precedent is shown to be a reason rather than a guarantee.

entries.pericope: Build houses; plant gardens; seek the peace of the city
entries.connection: The exiles are told to settle, marry, multiply, and pray for the welfare of the place holding them captive — because in its peace they will have peace. The Citizen-Stranger given its founding instruction, and the city in question is Babylon.

entries.pericope: You shall seek me and find me, when you search with all your heart
entries.connection: The famous promise of a future and a hope is attached to seventy years, not to relief — the plans are announced to people who will die before they see them. Seeking with the whole heart is the condition, and the timescale is the point.

entries.pericope: Refrain your voice from weeping; there is hope for your latter end
entries.connection: Rachel refusing comfort is answered rather than corrected — the weeping is addressed, given a reason to stop, and the reason is that the children come back. Then Ephraim is quoted bemoaning his own chastisement, and the response is that God's heart is troubled for him.

entries.pericope: Everyone shall die for his own iniquity
entries.connection: The proverb about fathers eating sour grapes and children's teeth being set on edge is retired by name. Inherited blame refused, and responsibility located in the person doing the eating.

entries.pericope: I will write it in their hearts
entries.connection: The new covenant is described by where the law is kept rather than by what it contains — put within them, written on the heart, so that teaching one another becomes unnecessary. Formation described as interior relocation, and it closes on forgiveness rather than on obedience.

entries.pericope: Houses and fields and vineyards shall yet again be bought in this land
entries.connection: He buys a field in a town already overrun, weighs out the silver, signs the deed before witnesses, and has it sealed in a clay jar to last a long time. Hope enacted as a property transaction conducted from inside a besieged city, with the paperwork done correctly.

entries.pericope: Ah Lord Yahweh; is there anything too hard for you?
entries.connection: Having obeyed, he immediately prays that he does not understand — the siege mounds are at the wall and he has just bought land. Obedience first and comprehension not at all, with the question left standing rather than answered.

entries.pericope: Call to me, and I will answer you
entries.connection: Spoken while he is still shut up in the court of the guard, and the promise is health, cure, and abundance of peace to a city about to fall. The invitation to call is issued to a man already imprisoned for the message.

entries.pericope: The Rechabites, who would not drink the wine
entries.connection: Wine is set before them in the temple itself and they decline, citing an instruction from an ancestor generations back. The point drawn is not abstinence but continuity — a command kept for two centuries by ordinary people, set against a nation that would not keep one delivered directly.

entries.pericope: The king cut it with the knife and cast it into the fire
entries.connection: Three or four columns at a time, cut off and burned while the fire is going, and the narrator records that the king and his servants were not afraid and did not tear their garments. Three men intercede and are ignored. Rejection performed as an administrative act.

entries.pericope: Take another scroll, and write in it all the former words
entries.connection: The response to the destroyed work is to do it again, with more added. No lament over the loss is recorded and no protection is promised for the second scroll.

entries.pericope: I am not falling away to the Chaldeans
entries.connection: Arrested at the gate on a false charge of desertion, beaten, and imprisoned in a vaulted cell. When the king asks secretly whether there is a word, he gives the same answer that put him there, and then asks not to be sent back to that house.

entries.pericope: Ebedmelech took the rags and the worn-out clothes
entries.connection: A foreign eunuch goes to the king unprompted, gets a hearing, and pulls a man out of a cistern with thirty helpers. The detail preserved is that he sent down old rags first, to pad the ropes under Jeremiah's armpits — kindness attending to what would have hurt.

entries.pericope: If I give you counsel, you will not listen to me
entries.connection: A private consultation in which the king wants the answer without the consequences and is afraid of his own officials. The prophet names the fear accurately, gives the counsel anyway, and then agrees to a cover story to keep them both alive.

entries.pericope: Because you have put your trust in me
entries.connection: The single promise of deliverance in the fall of the city goes to the Ethiopian who pulled him out of the mud. Delivered in the middle of a national catastrophe, to a foreigner, for one act.

entries.pericope: Whether it be good, or whether it be evil, we will obey
entries.connection: The remnant swears to obey whatever answer comes, before it comes, and calls God a true and faithful witness against them if they do not. Ten days pass before the word arrives.

entries.pericope: You dealt deceitfully against your own souls
entries.connection: They had decided before they asked. The charge is that they dealt deceitfully against their own souls — self-deception named as the mechanism, with the oath they swore ten days earlier quoted back to them.

entries.pericope: Do you seek great things for yourself? Don't seek them
entries.connection: Baruch has written the scroll twice, been hunted for it, and says he is weary with his groaning and finds no rest. The answer grants the exhaustion, refuses the ambition beneath it, and promises only his life as spoils wherever he goes. Five verses, and they are the whole of what the Hidden Life costs.

entries.pericope: They left of the poorest of the land to be vineyard keepers
entries.connection: The book closes with an inventory: the breach, the famine, the sons killed before their father's eyes, the eyes then put out, the house burned. And the poorest are left behind to tend the vines — the last detail recorded is who remained.

review_log.adjudication: Clean pass. PR01 accepted on 8:4-7; PR12 declined on 9:3-8.
Clean pass. PR06 accepted on 18:18-23; PR15 declined as duplicative; C17 declined on 13:1-11.
Clean pass. Two gap proposals declined, both on established precedents.

coverage_note: Chapters 34-52 are indexed selectively. The narrative material — the Rechabites, the burned scroll, the cistern, the flight to Egypt, Baruch's word, the fall — is covered. The oracles against the nations in chapters 46-51 are not: six chapters of judgment on Egypt, Moab, Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, Elam and Babylon, which on a plain reading anchor nothing in a curriculum of personal formation. Indexing them would have required either allegory or a stretched tag, and both were declined, as with the wasfs in Song of Solomon.
